mstts:express-as.prosody: As we wrap up, let’s bring it all together. Living abolition isn’t some far-off dream or just a single moment of protest. It’s a real, ongoing practice—a way of moving through life with care, with courage, and with a spark of imagination. This journey? It’s both shared and personal. It unfolds in your daily choices, in how you show up for others, and in the small acts of solidarity you make, day by day. So, what does it look like to live abolition in your own life and community? Here are a few guiding thoughts: First, try shifting from punishment to healing in how you respond to harm—even in ordinary moments. Invest in your relationships and mutual aid, because that’s truly the heart of safety. Don’t be afraid to question reforms that just reinforce the old systems—let yourself imagine what deeper transformation could look like. Practice real accountability and care, for yourself and with others. And remember to sustain this work—with rest, with reflection, and by sharing leadership. Abolition isn’t about being perfect, or expecting instant change. It’s about sticking with the process—honoring the dignity and potential of every person, and building systems rooted in care, not control. There’ll be setbacks, and sometimes the path ahead will feel unclear. But every act of solidarity, every moment of accountability, and every effort to meet needs without punishment—these are steps toward a more just and liberated world. Here’s something powerful: you’re not alone in this. Across generations and communities, people are imagining and building new ways of living together—ways that honor our shared humanity and our capacity for transformation. So trust in collective action. Nurture hope, even when it feels hard. And remember, every small act of care, every moment you choose compassion over control, is part of something so much bigger. The world we’re reaching for is already taking shape—one relationship, one community, and one act of courage at a time.
